claims.text: Conventional powder-consolidated or sintered W–Cu composites contain W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
A W–Cu graded interlayer can be deposited on W surfaces by physical vapor deposition before composite consolidation.
Increasing the interlayer thickness from 50–100 nm to approximately 200–300 nm, or tailoring its composition, will improve interfacial stability.
The proposed interlayer has a smoothly graded composition from pure W to Cu.
The graded interlayer will remain coherent and minimize abrupt compositional gradients at the W–Cu interface.
Minimizing abrupt compositional gradients will reduce interfacial stresses.
The graded interlayer will promote controlled atomic interdiffusion during sintering.
Controlled interdiffusion will eliminate sharp W–Cu interfaces and reduce their interfacial energy.
Reducing interfacial energy will suppress void nucleation and mitigate phase separation.
Suppressing voids and phase separation will enhance mechanical bonding and thermal contact at the W–Cu interface.
Improved interfacial thermal contact will increase the effective thermal conductivity relative to an untreated W–Cu composite.
The graded interlayer will provide more stable performance during prolonged high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically exhibit phase separation and interfacial void formation that limit thermal performance.
The proposed benefits apply after sintering at approximately 800 °C under an inert atmosphere.
The proposed benefits apply in service from 500 °C to 800 °C under Ar+, He+, or D+ ion irradiation.
The graded interface can maintain stability during thermal cycling and radiation exposure within the stated service window.
